{{User page}}

This is a proposal to add candidacy and election data for the November 2026
elections in the San Francisco Bay Area. It is a draft for discussion. One
contest has been done as a pilot; nothing further will be added until this has
had a hearing.

I would particularly like feedback on the modelling questions in
[[#Open questions|Open questions]] below — I am not an expert in how elections
are modelled here, and several of my choices are inferences from a small number
of existing items rather than anything I found written down.

=== Why I want this ===

I should be straightforward about my motivation, since it shapes what I am
asking for.

I want to build a feed that surfaces Wikipedia edits to the articles of people
standing for office in the Bay Area, during the campaign, so that changes to
candidate biographies are visible while they matter rather than afterwards. For
that feed to work without me hand-maintaining a list of people, it has to ask
Wikidata who the candidates are — which is why I care that these statements
exist and are correct.

Two things follow that are worth stating rather than leaving for someone to
discover. It means I have an interest in coverage being complete, which is a
reason to be sceptical of my scope choices. And it means an incorrect statement
does not sit quietly in a database: the feed would repeat the claim that someone
is a candidate off-wiki, where nobody here can revert it. That asymmetry is why
I have been more cautious about name resolution than the data-quality case alone
would justify.

The data seems to me worth having regardless — but if you think the feed is a
bad idea, I would rather hear that now, and the modelling questions below are
still worth answering either way.

== The gap ==

Wikidata knows very little about who is standing for office in the Bay Area this
November.

The election items that exist are close to empty. Before the pilot below,
{{Q|Q131470954}} carried {{P|P17}} and {{P|P31}} and nothing else — no date, no
jurisdiction, no office contested. {{Q|Q138112703}}, {{Q|Q139040246}} and
{{Q|Q139073833}} still carry only {{P|P31}}. Because they have no {{P|P585}} and
no {{P|P1001}}, they cannot be found by any query that does not already know
their QIDs.

Candidacy statements are almost entirely absent. This returns everyone with a
{{P|P3602}} to a 2026 election in California — three people, two of whom I added
in the pilot below:

{{SPARQL|query=SELECT ?person ?personLabel ?electionLabel WHERE {
  ?person p:P3602 ?st . ?st ps:P3602 ?election .
  ?election wdt:P1001 wd:Q99 ; wdt:P585 ?d .
  FILTER(YEAR(?d) = 2026)
  ?person wdt:P31 wd:Q5 .
  SERVICE wikibase:label { bd:serviceParam wikibase:language "en". }
}}}

Meanwhile {{P|P39}} is not a usable substitute. Querying current officeholders
whose position has {{P|P1001}} into any of the nine Bay Area counties returns 19
people, including ten concurrent Sheriffs of San Francisco and four concurrent
District Attorneys — the result of missing {{P|P582}} end dates accumulated over
many years.

== What I would like to add ==

Two kinds of statement.

'''Data-model statements on election items''' — {{P|P585}}, {{P|P1001}},
{{P|P541}}, and series links — bringing 2026 items to the same completeness as
the equivalent items for earlier cycles. Roughly 115–200 statements across
25–40 items, some of which do not exist yet and would need creating.

'''Candidacy statements''' linking people who ''already have items'' to the
contests they are standing in, each with a reference. Roughly 65–90 statements.

Total is in the low hundreds. This is not a bulk import, and I am not proposing
to create items for people.

=== What I am not proposing ===

* '''No new items for candidates.''' Around 26 of the candidates I have
  identified have no Wikidata item. Creating biographical items for largely
  private people from a single primary source is a different undertaking with
  different notability and living-person considerations, and I am not asking to
  do it. Those candidates are recorded as gaps and left alone.
* '''No bot, currently.''' Every statement so far has been made through
  QuickStatements from a batch I read first. Whether parts of this ''should'' be
  automated is one of the open questions below.

== The pilot: California's 11th congressional district ==

I did one contest end to end so there is something concrete to inspect rather
than only a description. This is Nancy Pelosi's open seat; Scott Wiener and
Connie Chan advanced from the June primary.

'''Data model''', on {{Q|Q131470954}} — five statements bringing it to parity
with {{Q|Q116006860}}, the 2024 equivalent, which already carried all of them:
{{P|P585}} 3 November 2026, {{P|P1001}} California, {{P|P541}} United States
representative, {{P|P361}}, {{P|P155}}.

'''Candidacies''', on {{Q|Q7437504}} and {{Q|Q105663114}}: {{P|P3602}} →
{{Q|Q131470954}}, qualified {{P|P768}} → {{Q|Q2681039}}, each referenced to the
certified Statement of Vote.

Both items' histories are public and I would welcome scrutiny of them.

=== An error, and how it was caught ===

I am describing this because it is the most useful thing I can tell you about
how reliable this process is.

Connie Chan's candidacy was first written to {{Q|Q110933376}} — which is a
disambiguation page, not a person. The QID had been resolved by looking up the
enwiki title "Connie Chan", which is itself a disambiguation page, and the
verification step compared ''labels'', which match on both items. The check
could not have caught the error.

It was found by a human asking whether the identifiers had actually been
validated, and corrected the following day: removed from {{Q|Q110933376}}, added
to {{Q|Q105663114}}, which is {{P|P31}} human and holds {{P|P39}} member of the
San Francisco Board of Supervisors.

Every subsequent resolution requires {{P|P31}} = {{Q|Q5}} as a hard gate, and
the checklist asks whether the item's dates and description are consistent with
a 2026 candidate.

== Sourcing ==

This is the part I am willing to commit to absolutely.

'''Every candidacy statement cites a source that directly supports it''' —
establishing that the person is on the November ballot, not merely that they
filed. In practice:

* For contests with a June primary, the certified '''Statement of Vote''', which
  shows who advanced under California's top-two rule. The certified ''list of
  candidates'' is not sufficient on its own: it names all eleven CA-11 primary
  candidates and does not distinguish the two who advanced.
* For contests whose first round is in November — many municipal offices — the
  general-election certified candidate list, which enumerates exactly the people
  on that ballot.

References carry {{P|P854}}, {{P|P1476}} and {{P|P813}}, plus {{P|P577}} only
where the source states a publication date.

'''{{P|P143}} is not used.''' The intended consumer of this data is a bot that
watches Wikipedia edits, so sourcing Wikidata back to Wikipedia would make
unsourced Wikipedia edits into "sourced" Wikidata.

== Automation and AI involvement ==

An LLM-assisted toolchain (Claude, driven interactively) parses the published
results spreadsheets, computes which districts overlap the Bay Area and who
advanced, proposes name→QID matches with scores, and generates QuickStatements
batches and the queries that verify them. It drafted this page.

'''It holds no credentials, has no account, and makes no edits.''' Everything so
far has gone through QuickStatements under this account, from a batch I read.

=== Measured error rates ===

Name resolution is where the risk is, and the numbers are not flattering.

{| class="wikitable"
! Method !! Matches returned !! Known wrong
|-
| Matching on label alone (52-candidate subset) || 30 || at least 5
|-
| Scored on {{P|P31}}/{{P|P39}}/{{P|P106}}/{{P|P27}} + sitelinks (full 67) || 32 || 1
|}

Label matching would have attached candidacies to an actor who died in 2002, a
cricketer born in 1868, and a film producer. Scoring is roughly an order of
magnitude better and still not zero: one candidate resolved confidently to a
19th-century labour leader, because he genuinely is an American with an
occupation, held positions and an article. Every signal fired correctly and the
answer was wrong.

That residual rate is why name resolution is reviewed by hand rather than
trusted, and it will not be tuned away.

== Open questions ==

These are the things I would most like input on. I have working answers, but
they are inferences and I would rather be corrected now than after several
hundred statements exist.

# '''Which stages, if any, should be automated?''' Risk is not uniform. Parsing
  certified results, writing data-model statements from a fixed template, and
  attaching references are ordinary data processing. Resolving a name to a QID
  is the stage with a measured error rate and living-person exposure. Is there
  an established view on where the line sits, and would a bot flag be
  appropriate for the mechanical parts?
# '''{{P|P3602}} on the person, or {{P|P726}} on the election?''' I have used
  {{P|P3602}} for congressional and legislative contests — there is no
  per-district election item for regular cycles to attach {{P|P726}} to — and
  intended {{P|P726}} for mayoral and council contests, following the New York
  City, Boston, Chicago and Los Angeles items. '''Four items is an observation,
  not a convention.''' Is mixing directions by contest type normal? Does
  {{P|P726}} become unwieldy for contests with many candidates?
# '''Should congressional and legislative district items carry {{P|P131}} to the
  counties they cover?''' They are currently modelled {{P|P131}} → the state, so
  there is no way to ask which districts are in a given region. Adding
  county-level {{P|P131}} would make it derivable, and is arguably accurate, but
  it is a modelling change across many items to suit one query and I would not
  do it unilaterally.
# '''What should a local election item be required to carry?''' The Bay Area
  items for earlier cycles are nearly empty, so I have taken the model from
  better-developed mayoral items elsewhere. Would an [[Wikidata:Schemas|
  EntitySchema]] for election items be welcome, and does one already exist?
# '''Are county- and city-level election items wanted at all?''' I read
  [[Wikidata:Notability]] criterion 2 as covering them — a certified election
  documented by an official canvass is clearly identifiable with public
  references. If that is wrong, most local coverage does not happen, and it is
  better to know now.
# '''Is the scope right?''' Currently federal, state legislative, county
  offices, and cities over 100,000 or county seats. Deliberately conservative.
  It could reasonably be called too narrow to be useful, or too broad given that
  candidates for smaller offices are closer to private individuals.

== Scope, briefly ==

Contests for offices representing part of the nine Bay Area counties: US House,
State Senate, State Assembly, county offices, and cities over 100,000 population
or county seats. Statewide offices are excluded — they are not specific to the
region. School boards, special districts, and smaller municipal offices are
excluded deliberately, on the grounds that candidates for them are closer to
private individuals than public figures.

== Objections, and what happens next ==

* '''A challenged statement is reverted first and discussed after.''' If
  something here is wrong, revert it; I will not restore it without discussing.
* '''Everything is published.''' The register of contests, the sources used, and
  every batch applied will be on-wiki as subpages of this page, so anyone can
  see what was added and on what evidence.
* '''Batches are small and incremental''', so an error affects a reviewable
  number of statements.

The full method, in more detail than belongs on this page, is at
[[/Method]].

Comments here or on the talk page are welcome. I intend to leave this for
discussion before adding anything beyond the CA-11 pilot.
